standard_text: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with fractional edge lengths using unit cubes of the appropriate unit fraction edge lengths (e.g., using technology or concrete materials) and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths of the prism. Apply the formulas V = lwh and V = Bh to find volumes of right rectangular prisms with fractional edge lengths to solve real-world and other mathematical problems.

progression.narrative: 6.GM.4 makes two demands, in a deliberate order. First, UNDERSTAND: show that volume with fractional edges still means filling space -- pack a prism with unit-fraction cubes and prove the packing count, converted to cubic units, is exactly what multiplying the edge lengths gives. Second, APPLY: use V = lwh and V = Bh fluently on real-world and mathematical problems. The progression follows that logic. A student first extends the familiar V = lwh to a single fractional edge (S1), where the layer picture still carries them. Then comes the standard's conceptual heart (S2): packing with 1/2-inch or 1/3-cm cubes and discovering that a small cube is NOT a cubic unit -- eight half-inch cubes make one cubic inch -- so count and volume finally separate. With that understanding secured, computation scales up to two and three fractional dimensions (S3), gets applied to real packing and filling contexts (S4), and folds into the V = Bh form, where the base area arrives pre-multiplied (S5). The capstone (S6) runs the formula in reverse -- given the volume, recover a missing edge or propose possible dimensions -- which is where this standard hands off to grade-7 geometry and to equation thinking. Two foundations sit underneath: fraction multiplication (F1), because every item here ends in it, and the grade-5 image of volume as counting unit cubes (F2), because every idea here is built on it.

steps.rationale: Extend V = lwh to one fractional edge. The layer picture from grade 5 still works -- a 1/2-unit height is half a layer -- so this is the gentlest entry into the standard's 'fractional edge lengths' demand, and the first place the add-the-edges habit must be broken.

The standard's own words: pack with unit-fraction cubes AND show the result equals multiplying the edges. The insight that 8 half-inch cubes make one cubic inch is what separates cube COUNT from VOLUME -- everything after leans on it.

Full computational demand: V = lwh with two or three fractional or mixed-number dimensions -- the spec's medium and difficult tiers. Three messy factors is where the third dimension silently drops, so this step trains the three-factor habit.

The standard says 'to solve real-world and other mathematical problems.' Packing dice, filling sandboxes -- volume and cube-packing now do work inside a story, and answers must be counts or cubic units as the question demands.
The second named formula, V = Bh. Students must read B as a finished AREA -- l x w folded into one number -- which prepares them for prisms with non-rectangular bases in grade 7.

The spec's Above tier reverses the formula: given the volume, recover a missing edge or propose possible dimensions. Undoing multiplication with division is the bridge from this standard to equation solving and 7.GM.3.

skills.name: Multiply fractions, whole numbers, and mixed numbers accurately

prerequisite_skill.description: Multiply a fraction by a fraction and a fraction by a whole number

skills.i_do_script: Every volume problem in this standard ends with multiplying fractions, so that move has to be solid first. Model 2 1/2 x 1 1/2 out loud: rewrite each mixed number as an improper fraction (5/2 and 3/2), multiply straight across to get 15/4, and rename it 3 3/4. Do NOT multiply the whole parts and fraction parts separately -- show the student why 2 x 1 = 2 plus 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4 misses the two cross pieces.

canonical_error.pattern: Multiplies the whole-number parts and the fraction parts of mixed numbers separately
canonical_error.example: For 2 1/2 x 1 1/2, student computes 2 x 1 = 2 and 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4, then answers 2 1/4 instead of 3 3/4
canonical_error.why: The student treats a mixed number as two separate numbers instead of one quantity. Multiplication distributes over BOTH parts of BOTH numbers, so splitting them drops the two cross products (2 x 1/2 and 1 x 1/2).

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- mixed numbers can't be split like that.
redirect_script.prompt: Rewrite each mixed number as an improper fraction first. 2 1/2 is 5/2 and 1 1/2 is 3/2. Now multiply straight across: top times top, bottom times bottom. What do you get?
redirect_script.praise: You converted to improper fractions and multiplied straight across -- that method never misses a piece.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 2 1/2 x 1 1/2 = ?
Before we compute -- estimate. 2 1/2 groups of 1 1/2: should the answer be bigger or smaller than 2 1/2? Why?
Mixed numbers are sneaky to multiply, so we rename them first. 2 1/2 means 5 halves, so we write 5/2. 1 1/2 means 3 halves, so we write 3/2.
Now that both are plain fractions, how do we multiply two fractions?
Write: 5/2 x 3/2 = 15/4. Top times top, bottom times bottom.
15/4 is an improper fraction. How many whole ones are hiding in 15 fourths, and what's left over?

If the student had answered 2 1/4 at the start (2 x 1 and 1/2 x 1/2), don't just correct it -- compare it to the estimate. 2 1/4 is smaller than 2 1/2, but we agreed the answer had to be BIGGER. Let that contradiction drive the fix.
So 2 1/2 x 1 1/2 = 3 3/4. Convert to improper fractions, multiply straight across, rename. Same three moves every time.

skills.name: Understand volume as the count of unit cubes filling a prism

prerequisite_skill.description: Recognize volume as an attribute measured by packing a solid with unit cubes (5.M.4/5.M.5)
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A box holds 2 layers of 6 cubes each. How many cubes fill the box?

skills.i_do_script: Volume answers one question: how many unit cubes fit inside with no gaps? Model with a 4 x 3 x 2 box: the bottom layer is 4 rows of 3, so 12 cubes, and there are 2 layers, so 24 cubes -- the volume is 24 cubic units. Say 'layer' out loud every time; the layer picture is what makes V = l x w x h feel obvious instead of magical.

canonical_error.pattern: Combines the three dimensions additively instead of seeing layers of cubes
canonical_error.example: For a box 4 units by 3 units by 2 units, student answers 9 (4 + 3 + 2) instead of 24
canonical_error.why: The student sees three labeled numbers and reaches for the most familiar way to combine them -- addition. They haven't built the image of a layer of cubes (4 x 3) repeated 2 times, which is what makes volume multiplicative.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- let's build it instead of adding it.
redirect_script.prompt: Picture just the bottom layer of cubes. How many rows, and how many cubes in each row? Multiply those to count one layer. Now, how many layers stack up to the top? Multiply again.
redirect_script.praise: You counted a layer and stacked it -- that's exactly what volume means.

worked_example_script.text: Sketch (or display) a box labeled 4 units long, 3 units wide, 2 units tall.

So how many cubes are in that one layer? What operation did you just use?
The box is 2 units tall. How many of those layers stack inside it?
12 cubes per layer, 2 layers -- how many cubes in all?

If the student says 9, they added 4 + 3 + 2. Hand them 24 linking cubes (or draw the layers) and have them physically build the bottom layer -- the addition answer collapses the moment they see 12 cubes in one layer alone.
24 cubes means the volume is 24 cubic units. Volume is a COUNT of cubes -- length times width counts one layer, and height counts the layers.
Without building it, how many unit cubes would fill a 5 by 2 by 3 box? Talk me through the layers.

skills.name: Calculate the volume of a prism with one fractional edge
skills.i_do_script: We're using V = l x w x h on a prism where one edge is a fraction. Model with a box 6 in. by 4 in. by 1/2 in.: the base layer is 6 x 4 = 24, and the height 1/2 means only half of that layer's worth of space, so 24 x 1/2 = 12 cubic inches. Point at each labeled edge on the figure as you use it -- students must see that all THREE numbers get multiplied, never added.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds the three edge lengths instead of multiplying them
canonical_error.example: For a prism 6 in. x 4 in. x 1/2 in., student answers 10 1/2 (6 + 4 + 1/2) instead of 12 cubic inches
canonical_error.why: Three labeled numbers on a figure trigger the perimeter habit of combining by adding. The student hasn't anchored volume to the layer picture -- a 6 x 4 layer of cubes taken 1/2 time -- so the formula's multiplication feels arbitrary and addition sneaks in.

redirect_script.stop: Stop -- did you add those edges or multiply them?
redirect_script.prompt: Volume is multiplying, never adding. Write the formula V = l x w x h first, then copy one labeled number under each letter. Multiply the two whole numbers first, then multiply by the fraction.
redirect_script.praise: You wrote the formula, matched every edge to a letter, and multiplied all three. That's the whole skill.

Which two numbers would you multiply first to keep it easy? What is 6 x 4?
Now 24 x 1/2 -- taking half of 24. What do you get?

activities.title: Half-Layer Build
activities.instructions:
1. Groups build a 6-by-4 layer of cubes and count it (24).
2. Say: our prism is only HALF this tall. Ask groups to show what half a layer looks like (split the layer in two, keep one part).
3. Groups write the number sentence that matches what they built: 6 x 4 x 1/2 = 12.
4. Repeat with a 5-by-2 layer and a height of 1 1/2 (one full layer plus a half layer).
5. Debrief: why does the height tell us how many LAYERS, even when it's a fraction?

activities.title: Add or Multiply?
activities.instructions:
1. Show Marcus's work; pairs decide what he did with the three labeled edges.
2. Pairs write the correct formula V = l x w x h and recompute.
3. Debrief question: what does adding the edges measure -- anything at all? (Edge lengths laid end to end, not space.)

content.worked_problem: A prism is 7 in. long, 2 in. wide, and 1/2 in. tall. Marcus wrote: V = 7 + 2 + 1/2 = 9 1/2 cubic inches.
content.error_step: Marcus added the three edge lengths instead of multiplying them.
content.why: Volume counts the cubes inside: a 7 x 2 layer holds 14, and a 1/2-unit height means half a layer, so V = 7 x 2 x 1/2 = 7 cubic inches. Adding edges never counts space.

activities.title: Prism-to-Volume Match
materials: Card set (dimension cards and volume cards)
activities.instructions:
1. Deal the dimension cards face up and the volume cards face down in a pool.
2. Pairs flip a volume card and race to match it to the prism dimensions that produce it.
3. Every match must be defended out loud with V = l x w x h.
4. The decoys are sums of the edges -- if a pair grabs one, have them check by multiplying.

strategy_links.why: The added-the-edges error is concrete and visible -- find-and-fix work makes students articulate why volume multiplies.
Building half-layers with cubes grounds the fractional height before the formula goes abstract.
The formula routine (write V = lwh, match numbers, multiply) transfers cleanly through I-do / we-do / you-do.

skills.name: Show that packing unit-fraction cubes matches multiplying the edges
skills.i_do_script: This is the 'show it two ways' skill: pack a prism with small cubes AND multiply the edges, and prove both give the same volume. Model with a 2 in. x 1 in. x 1 in. prism packed with 1/2-inch cubes: it holds 4 x 2 x 2 = 16 little cubes, but each little cube is only 1/2 x 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/8 cubic inch, so the volume is 16 x 1/8 = 2 cubic inches -- exactly what 2 x 1 x 1 gives. The trap to expose: 16 cubes is NOT 16 cubic inches.

canonical_error.pattern: Reports the count of small cubes as the volume in cubic units
canonical_error.example: A 2 in. x 1 in. x 1 in. prism packs 16 half-inch cubes; student answers 16 cubic inches instead of 2 cubic inches
canonical_error.why: In grade 5 every packing cube WAS a unit cube, so count and volume were the same number. The student carries that habit over and assumes each small cube is 1 cubic unit, when a 1/2-inch cube is actually only 1/8 of a cubic inch.

redirect_script.stop: Careful -- those little cubes aren't 1 cubic inch each.
redirect_script.prompt: Ask yourself: how many of these small cubes stack up to make one REAL cubic inch? A 1/2-inch cube takes 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 of them. So divide your cube count by 8 -- or skip the cubes entirely and multiply the edge lengths.
redirect_script.praise: You converted cube count into cubic units -- and it matched l x w x h exactly. That's the big idea of this standard.

practice_problems.stem: Why does it take 8 half-inch cubes -- not 2 -- to fill 1 cubic inch? Explain or draw.
practice_problems.answer: A cubic inch is 1 inch in ALL THREE directions. Half-inch cubes fit 2 along the length, 2 along the width, and 2 up the height: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8. Halving happens in three directions at once, not one.

activities.title: Build a Cubic Inch
activities.instructions:

3. Now pack a 2 in. x 1 in. x 1 in. box: count the cubes (16) and convert to cubic inches (16 x 1/8 = 2).
4. Check by formula: 2 x 1 x 1 = 2. Same answer.
5. Debrief: when does the cube count equal the volume, and when doesn't it?

activities.title: Match My Volume
activities.instructions:
1. Player A names a small-cube edge (spin or roll) and a cube count that makes a 'nice' volume (for example, 1/2-in cubes and 16 cubes).
2. Player B computes the volume in cubic units (16 x 1/8 = 2 cubic inches).
3. Player A checks by proposing prism dimensions that multiply to the same volume (2 x 1 x 1).
4. Swap roles. One point per verified match; the pair's score is shared -- accuracy over speed.

worked_example_script.text: Display a prism figure labeled l = 2 1/2 in., w = 4 in., h = 1 1/2 in.

Write V = l x w x h, then V = 2 1/2 x 4 x 1 1/2. Put a check on each edge of the figure as its number goes into the line.
Which two numbers would you multiply first to make this easiest? Why is 2 1/2 x 4 a friendly start?

This is the danger moment -- students write 10 and stop. If that happens, point at the figure: 'You have three checks to earn and only two so far. Which edge hasn't been used?'

strategy_links.why: The dropped-dimension error produces work that LOOKS right for two steps -- students need practice catching it in finished solutions.

skills.name: Solve real-world cube-packing and volume problems
skills.i_do_script: Now the volume work lives inside a story: how many dice fill the box, how much sand fills the sandbox. Model the dice problem two ways for a box 3 in. x 2 in. x 1 in. with 1/2-inch dice: (1) count along each edge -- 6 dice fit along the 3-inch length, 4 along the width, 2 up the height, so 6 x 4 x 2 = 48 dice; (2) volumes -- the box is 6 cubic inches, each die is 1/8 cubic inch, and 6 divided by 1/8 is 48. The trap: dividing 6 by 1/2 (the edge) instead of 1/8 (the die's volume).

canonical_error.pattern: Divides the box's volume by the cube's edge length instead of the cube's volume
canonical_error.example: Box 3 in. x 2 in. x 1 in. filled with 1/2-inch dice: student computes 6 / (1/2) = 12 dice instead of 6 / (1/8) = 48
canonical_error.why: The student remembers 'divide by the cube' but grabs the number printed in the problem (the edge, 1/2) instead of cubing it first. A 1/2-inch die occupies 1/8 cubic inch -- volume divided by volume gives a count; volume divided by a length does not.

redirect_script.stop: Pause -- is 1/2 that die's VOLUME, or just its edge?
redirect_script.prompt: Before you divide, find the volume of ONE cube: edge x edge x edge. Write it down and label it. Now divide the box's volume by that cube volume -- or skip division and count cubes along each edge instead.
redirect_script.praise: You divided volume by volume -- cubic inches by cubic inches -- and got a clean count. Units don't lie.

The edge measurements of a cube or prism.

worked_example_script.text: Display: 'A box is 3 in. long, 2 in. wide, and 1 in. tall. It is filled with dice that are cubes with 1/2-inch sides. How many dice fill the box?' Show the labeled prism figure.
Before any math: about how many dice do you think fit? More than 10? More than 100? Just estimate.
How many 1/2-inch dice fit along the 3-inch length? How did you get that?
How many fit along the 2-inch width? Up the 1-inch height?
Write: 6 x 4 x 2 = 48 dice.
Now the second road, with volumes. The box holds 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 cubic inches. One die is 1/2 x 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/8 cubic inch. How many 1/8s are in 6? That's 6 divided by 1/8 = 48. Same answer.
If a student divides 6 by 1/2 and says 12, ask: 'Is 1/2 the die's volume or just one edge? What is the whole die's volume?' The units catch it: cubic inches must be divided by cubic inches.
Which road do you like better -- counting along edges or dividing volumes? When might you need the division road?

skills.name: Apply V = Bh using the area of the base
skills.i_do_script: V = Bh is the same volume idea folded in half: B is the AREA of the base (a whole layer, already multiplied), and h counts the layers. Model with a base of 4 cm by 3 cm and a height of 2 1/2 cm: B = 4 x 3 = 12 square cm, then V = 12 x 2 1/2 = 30 cubic cm. Then show the shortcut case: if the problem already SAYS the base area is 12, you skip straight to 12 x 2 1/2. The capital B is an area, never an edge.

canonical_error.pattern: Finds the base area B by adding the base's length and width instead of multiplying
canonical_error.example: Base 4 cm by 3 cm, height 2 1/2 cm: student writes B = 4 + 3 = 7 and V = 7 x 2 1/2 = 17 1/2 instead of B = 12 and V = 30
canonical_error.why: The phrase 'the base' pulls up perimeter-flavored thinking -- combining the two edges additively. The student hasn't locked in that B is an AREA: squares covering the bottom, which requires length x width.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- is B the distance around the base, or the squares covering it?
redirect_script.prompt: B is the AREA of the base: the number of unit squares covering the bottom. Draw the base as a rectangle, and find how many squares cover it -- length TIMES width. Then multiply by the height.
redirect_script.praise: You found B as an area -- squares covering the base -- and then stacked it with the height. That's V = Bh working perfectly.

skills.item_template: Either the base area B is given directly with a (often fractional) height, or the base's length and width are given and the student finds B first. Apply V = Bh. NR (numeric response).

vocabulary.definition: The face a prism sits on -- for V = Bh it's the bottom rectangle.
The area of the base face, in SQUARE units; the capital B in V = Bh.
How tall the prism is -- the distance from base to top.
Areas are labeled in square units; volumes are labeled in cubic units.

worked_example_script.text: Display a prism with its base labeled 4 cm by 3 cm and its height labeled 2 1/2 cm. Write both formulas side by side: V = l x w x h and V = B x h.
These two formulas give the same volume. Looking at them, what do you think the capital B stands for?
The base is 4 cm by 3 cm. How many unit SQUARES cover that base? Is that adding or multiplying?
Write B = 4 x 3 = 12 sq cm. Shade the base on the figure.
If a student says B = 7, they added 4 + 3. Sketch the base as a 4-by-3 grid and count the squares -- 12, not 7. Adding gives you edge lengths laid end to end, not covering.
Now V = B x h = 12 x 2 1/2. What does multiplying by 2 1/2 mean in the layer picture?
What is 12 x 2 1/2? (Twelve, twice, plus half of twelve.)
V = 30 cubic cm. And here's the shortcut: if a problem hands you 'the base area is 12 sq cm,' the multiplying is already done -- go straight to 12 x 2 1/2. B is always an area, never an edge.

practice_problems.stem: The base of a prism has an area of 10 sq cm. The prism is 2 cm tall. Use V = Bh to find the volume in cubic centimeters.
A prism's base is 3 cm long and 2 cm wide. What is B, the area of the base, in square centimeters?
The base of a rectangular prism has an area of 14 sq in. The prism is 1 1/2 in. tall. What is its volume in cubic inches?
A prism's base is 4 1/2 cm by 2 cm, and its height is 3 cm. Find B, then use V = Bh to find the volume.
practice_problems.answer: B = 9 sq cm; V = 27 cubic centimeters

practice_problems.stem: A prism's base is 5 in. by 4 in., and its height is 1 1/2 in. Kira used V = Bh. Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: 30 cubic inches. B is the AREA of the base -- multiply, don't add: B = 5 x 4 = 20 sq in., then V = 20 x 1 1/2 = 30.
practice_problems.notes: The added-base-edges error with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: The base of a prism has an area of 7 1/2 sq ft. The prism is 2 ft tall. What is its volume in cubic feet?
Prism A has base area 10 sq in. and height 3 in. Prism B has base area 15 sq in. and height 2 in. Which has the greater volume? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: Neither -- they're equal. A: 10 x 3 = 30 cubic inches; B: 15 x 2 = 30 cubic inches. A wider base with a shorter height can hold exactly the same space.
practice_problems.notes: Compare-and-explain stretch.

practice_problems.stem: A prism has a volume of 9 cubic cm and a height of 1 1/2 cm. Use V = Bh to find the area of its base, in square centimeters.
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction -- previews 6GM4-S6.

activities.title: Two Formulas, One Volume
activities.instructions:
1. Lay out three columns of cards: prism dimensions, a V = Bh setup, and a volume.
2. Pairs build complete matches: dimensions -> the matching B and h -> the volume.
3. Every match must be read aloud as 'B is ___ BECAUSE ___ times ___.'
4. Debrief: what is B, and what units does it wear?

pairs.left: Base 4 cm x 3 cm, height 2 1/2 cm
Base 5 in. x 2 in., height 1 1/2 in.
Base area 8 sq ft, height 3/4 ft
Base 3 1/2 ft x 2 ft, height 2 ft

activities.title: What Is B, Really?
activities.instructions:
1. Show Sam's work; pairs decide what his '10' measures.
2. Pairs draw the 6-by-4 base on grid paper and COUNT the squares covering it.
3. Redo the volume with the counted B.
4. Debrief question: what does 6 + 4 measure on the drawing? (Two edges laid end to end -- not covering.)

content.worked_problem: A prism's base is 6 cm by 4 cm and its height is 1/2 cm. Sam wrote: B = 6 + 4 = 10, so V = 10 x 1/2 = 5 cubic centimeters.
content.error_step: Sam added the base's length and width to get B instead of multiplying.
content.why: B is the AREA of the base -- the unit squares covering it: 6 x 4 = 24 sq cm. So V = 24 x 1/2 = 12 cubic centimeters.

activities.title: Stack the Base
materials: A stack of identical rectangles (index cards work)
activities.instructions:
1. Groups cut a 4-by-3 base from grid paper and count its squares (B = 12).
2. Stack index cards on the base: each card is one 'layer' of the prism.
3. Ask: if each card were 1 cm thick and we stacked 2 1/2 cards' worth, how much space is that? (12 x 2 1/2.)
4. Debrief: V = Bh means 'a base's worth of cubes, h times.' What changes if the height is a fraction?

strategy_links.why: 'What is B, and why isn't it 7?' is a perfect turn-and-talk -- students must verbalize area vs. added edges.
The B = l + w error hides inside otherwise-correct work; find-and-fix keeps students inspecting the B line.
The two-step routine (find B, then multiply by h) hands off cleanly from modeling to guided to independent work.

questioning_prompts: What does the capital B stand for -- an edge, a distance around, or an area?
What units does B wear? What units does the volume wear?
The problem already gave you the base area. What multiplication is already done for you?
Where is the base on this figure? Shade it before you compute.
How is V = Bh the same as V = l x w x h? Where did l x w go?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student computes B by adding the base's length and width -- e.g., B = 4 + 3 = 7 for a 4 cm by 3 cm base.
misconception_redirects.say: B is the AREA of the base: the number of unit squares covering the bottom. Draw the base as a rectangle, and find how many squares cover it -- length TIMES width. Then multiply by the height.
misconception_redirects.praise: You found B as an area -- squares covering the base -- and then stacked it with the height. That's V = Bh working perfectly.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student is given B directly (say, 12 sq in.) but stalls hunting for a length and width, or multiplies B by both a made-up l and w.
misconception_redirects.say: The problem already did l x w for you -- that's what 12 square inches IS. One multiplication left: B times the height.
misconception_redirects.praise: You recognized B as a finished area and went straight to B x h. Efficient and correct.

quick_checks.prompt: A base is 5 by 2. Tell me B -- and tell me what B is NOT.
quick_checks.look_for: 'B = 10 square units; it's not 7 (that's adding the edges).' Hearing the contrast confirms the area meaning stuck.

quick_checks.prompt: Base area 6 sq cm, height 1/2 cm. Volume, in one line?
quick_checks.look_for: V = 6 x 1/2 = 3 cubic cm. A 6 1/2 diagnoses adding B and h; hunting for more numbers diagnoses not trusting B as an area.

worked_solution.stem: A prism's base is 4 cm by 3 cm, and its height is 2 1/2 cm. Use V = Bh to find its volume.

steps.annotation: B is the AREA of the base -- unit squares covering the bottom. Multiply the base edges, never add them.
The height counts how many base-layers stack up -- here, two and a half layers.
12 x 2 = 24, and half of 12 is 6. Add the pieces.
B wore square units; the volume wears CUBIC units.

faded_example.stem: A prism's base is 5 in. by 2 in., and its height is 1 1/2 in. Use V = Bh to find its volume.

steps.annotation: Find the base AREA first: multiply the base edges.
Set up V = B x h with your base area and the height.
Multiply and label in cubic units.

sentence_starters: B = ___ square units because the base is ___ times ___.
V = Bh worked because B already holds l x w -- then I multiplied by the height.

skills.name: Find a missing dimension or possible dimensions from a known volume
skills.i_do_script: Now we run the volume formula in reverse: the volume is known, and an edge is missing. Model with V = 15 cubic inches, length 3 in., width 2 1/2 in.: the two known edges give 3 x 2 1/2 = 7 1/2, and the missing height must satisfy 7 1/2 x h = 15, so h = 15 divided by 7 1/2 = 2 inches. Always finish with the forward check: 3 x 2 1/2 x 2 = 15. If a student multiplies everything in sight, the check exposes it immediately.

canonical_error.pattern: Multiplies the volume by the known edges instead of dividing
canonical_error.example: V = 15 cubic inches, l = 3 in., w = 2 1/2 in.: student computes 15 x 3 x 2 1/2 = 112 1/2 instead of h = 15 / (3 x 2 1/2) = 2
canonical_error.why: Years of volume problems trained one reflex: multiply all the numbers. The student doesn't re-read the problem to notice the volume is now GIVEN and an edge is missing -- the formula must be undone with division, not run forward again.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- which number in this problem is the volume?
redirect_script.prompt: Circle the volume -- it's the ANSWER to l x w x h, not one of the edges. Write (known edge) x (known edge) x h = volume, multiply the two known edges, then divide the volume by that product to free h. Check by multiplying forward.
redirect_script.praise: You undid the formula with division and your forward check landed right on the volume. That's algebra thinking.

skills.item_template: The volume is given with two edges (or the base area), and the student finds the missing dimension; OR a cube count and unit-fraction edge are given, and the student finds the volume and proposes possible dimensions. NR or multi-part, spec Above Proficiency shape.

sample_items.stem:
A rectangular prism has a volume of 15 cubic inches. Its length is 3 in. and its width is 2 1/2 in.

What is the height, h, of the prism, in inches?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Watch for 112 1/2 (multiplying the volume by the known edges instead of dividing) or 9 1/2 (subtracting)

sample_items.stem:
A rectangular prism has a volume of 6 cubic centimeters. Its length is 4 cm and its width is 1/2 cm.

What is the height, h, of the prism, in centimeters?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Watch for 12 (multiplying everything) or 1 1/2 (dividing by only one known edge)

sample_items.stem:
A worker packs 64 cube-shaped boxes, each with side lengths of 1/4 ft, into a crate with no gaps. The crate is a rectangular prism.

Part A: What is the volume, in cubic feet, of the crate?

Part B: What are possible dimensions, in feet, of the crate?
sample_items.answer: Part A: 1 cubic foot | Part B: Answers vary; one possibility is 2 ft x 2 ft x 1/4 ft (any three multiples of 1/4 whose product is 1)
sample_items.distractor_logic: Part A watch-for: 16 (multiplying the count by the EDGE instead of the cube's volume). Part B: dimensions must each be a multiple of 1/4 and multiply to 1

sample_items.stem:
A rectangular prism has a volume of 10 1/2 cubic feet. The area of its base is 7 sq ft.

Use V = Bh to find the height, h, of the prism, in feet.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Watch for 73 1/2 (multiplying V by B) or 3 1/2 (subtracting)

vocabulary.definition: The unlabeled edge you solve for when the volume is already known.
A letter, like h, standing in for the number you're finding.
Operations that undo each other -- division undoes multiplication.
Any set of three edge lengths whose product equals the given volume.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 7.GM.3 -- volume and surface area of more complex solids.

worked_example_script.text: Display: 'A prism has a volume of 15 cubic inches. Its length is 3 in. and its width is 2 1/2 in. What is its height?' Show the figure with h = ? on the height edge.
Read carefully: which of these numbers is the VOLUME, and which are edges? How can you tell?
In past problems we multiplied three edges to GET the volume. What's different about what we know this time?
Write: 3 x 2 1/2 x h = 15.
What do the two known edges multiply to? So what times 7 1/2 equals 15?

If a student starts computing 15 x 3 x 2 1/2, stop the pencil: 'You just used 15 as an edge. Is 15 an edge or the finished volume?' Reread the stem together and re-sort the numbers before any arithmetic.
h = 15 / 7 1/2. How many 7 1/2s fit in 15?
h = 2 inches. Now the payoff habit -- check forward: 3 x 2 1/2 x 2 = 15. The check turns 'I think' into 'I know.'

practice_problems.stem: A prism's base area is 4 sq cm and its volume is 12 cubic cm. What is its height, in centimeters?
A prism has volume 8 cubic ft, length 4 ft, and width 2 ft. What is its height, in feet?
A prism has a volume of 9 cubic inches. Its length is 4 in. and its width is 1 1/2 in. What is its height, in inches?
practice_problems.notes: Watch for 54 (9 x 4 x 1 1/2) -- the multiply-everything reflex.

practice_problems.stem: A prism has a volume of 5 cubic cm. Its length is 2 1/2 cm and its width is 2 cm. What is its height, in centimeters?
A prism has a volume of 12 cubic feet, a length of 4 ft, and a width of 1 1/2 ft. Owen tried to find the height. Find his mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: 2 ft. Owen multiplied the volume by the edges -- but 12 is the finished volume, not an edge. Undo the formula: 4 x 1 1/2 = 6, and h = 12 / 6 = 2. Check: 4 x 1 1/2 x 2 = 12. (A 72-ft-tall prism holding only 12 cubic feet makes no sense.)
practice_problems.notes: The multiply-everything error with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: Exactly 40 cubes with 1/2-inch edges fill a box with no gaps. What is the volume of the box, in cubic inches?
A crate has a volume of 3 cubic feet, and every edge is a whole-number multiple of 1/2 ft. Give one possible set of dimensions for the crate.
practice_problems.answer: Answers vary. One possibility: 3 ft x 2 ft x 1/2 ft (3 x 2 x 1/2 = 3). Any three multiples of 1/2 whose product is 3 work.
practice_problems.notes: Produce-your-own -- spec Above shape, Part B.

practice_problems.stem: A prism's volume doubles, but its base area stays exactly the same. What happened to its height? Explain using V = Bh.
practice_problems.answer: The height doubled. In V = Bh, if B is unchanged and V doubles, h must double to keep the equation true -- height is the only factor left to carry the change.
practice_problems.notes: Reasoning about the formula's structure -- looking-forward thinking.

activities.title: Mystery Edge
activities.instructions:
1. Player A secretly picks three dimension cards, computes the volume, and reveals the volume plus TWO of the cards.
2. Player B finds the hidden edge and must say the division they used out loud.
3. Player A confirms by showing the hidden card; both check forward with l x w x h.
4. Swap roles. Score a point per correct recovery WITH a spoken forward check.

activities.title: Is 72 Feet Reasonable?
activities.instructions:
1. Show Owen's work (h = 12 x 4 x 1 1/2 = 72 ft) without comment.
2. First question to pairs: before checking any arithmetic, could a 72-foot-tall prism hold only 12 cubic feet? Why not?
3. Pairs sort the numbers (which is the volume? which are edges?), rewrite as 6 x h = 12, and solve.
4. Debrief: what reflex caused the error? (Multiply-everything.) What habit catches it? (Reasonableness + forward check.)

content.worked_problem: V = 12 cubic ft, l = 4 ft, w = 1 1/2 ft. Owen wrote: h = 12 x 4 x 1 1/2 = 72 ft.
content.error_step: Owen treated the given volume as another edge and multiplied everything together.
content.why: The volume is the RESULT of l x w x h. With V known, divide: 4 x 1 1/2 = 6, so h = 12 / 6 = 2 ft. The forward check 4 x 1 1/2 x 2 = 12 confirms it.

activities.title: Crate Designer
materials: A 'client order' card: 96 cube boxes, each with 1/4-ft edges
activities.instructions:
1. The client needs a crate that EXACTLY fits 96 cube boxes with 1/4-ft edges, no gaps.
2. Groups first find the crate's volume (96 x 1/64 = 1 1/2 cubic ft).
3. Each group designs TWO different crates (three dimensions each, every dimension a multiple of 1/4 ft) and verifies each design multiplies to 1 1/2.
4. Groups trade designs and check each other's with a forward multiplication.
5. Debrief: how many correct designs exist? Why more than one? (Volume fixes the product, not the shape.)

strategy_links.why: Studying a correct undo-the-formula solution next to the multiply-everything error is the fastest way to install the sorting step.
'Which number is the volume, and how do you know?' is the think-pair-share question this whole skill hinges on.
A think-aloud that sorts the givens (volume vs. edges) BEFORE computing models the self-questioning that prevents the reflex multiply.

questioning_prompts: Which number in this problem is the volume? Circle it before you touch your pencil.
What equation connects what you know to what's missing? Write it with the ? in place.
You divided -- by what, and why that number?
Check forward: multiply all three edges. Do you land on the given volume?
Is your answer reasonable -- could a prism with these edges really hold that volume?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student multiplies the given volume by the known edges -- e.g., h = 15 x 3 x 2 1/2 -- instead of dividing.
misconception_redirects.say: Circle the volume -- it's the ANSWER to l x w x h, not one of the edges. Write (known edge) x (known edge) x h = volume, multiply the two known edges, then divide the volume by that product to free h. Check by multiplying forward.
misconception_redirects.praise: You undid the formula with division and your forward check landed right on the volume. That's algebra thinking.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides the volume by only ONE known edge and stops -- e.g., h = 15 / 3 = 5.
misconception_redirects.say: Two edges are known, so combine them first: 3 x 2 1/2 = 7 1/2. THAT product is what h multiplies. Divide the volume by 7 1/2.
misconception_redirects.praise: You combined both known edges before dividing -- the missing edge came out clean, and the check proves it.

quick_checks.prompt: V = 10 cubic cm, l = 4 cm, w = 1/2 cm. Write ONLY the equation with h in it -- don't solve.
quick_checks.look_for: 4 x 1/2 x h = 10 (or h = 10 / 2). Anything starting '10 x 4' diagnoses the multiply-everything reflex.

quick_checks.prompt: You found h = 3. The edges were 2 and 1 1/2, volume 9. Prove your h in one line.
quick_checks.look_for: The forward check 2 x 1 1/2 x 3 = 9. Students who can't produce the check are guessing at the division.

worked_solution.stem: A prism has a volume of 15 cubic inches. Its length is 3 in. and its width is 2 1/2 in. What is its height?

steps.annotation: Sort the numbers first: 15 is the VOLUME (the product), 3 and 2 1/2 are edges, h is missing.
Combine the two known edges: 3 x 2 1/2 = 7 1/2.
Division undoes multiplication -- how many 7 1/2s make 15? Two.
Run the formula forward with your answer. Landing on 15 proves h = 2 in.

steps.annotation: Write the formula with the known edges and the missing h.
Combine the known edges first.
Divide the volume by that product to find h.
Check forward: multiply all three edges and confirm the volume.

foundation.label: Foundation
foundation.description: Tier III -- prerequisite skills from grade 5. If a student can't access Looking Back, start here.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: The easiest on-standard work -- one fractional edge. Fix this first if grade-level items are out of reach.

on_grade.label: On Grade
on_grade.description: Core 6.GM.4 skills -- packing with unit-fraction cubes, V = lwh with fractional dimensions, real-world problems, and V = Bh.

looking_forward.label: Looking Forward
looking_forward.description: Extension -- reverse the formula to find missing dimensions. The bridge to 7.GM.3.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S3 (V = lwh with fractional dimensions) -- the standard's computational center. If they pass, check the applications and the reverse direction (S4, S5, then S6). If they fail, drop back to S1 (one fractional edge) and the conceptual anchor S2; a student who can't do S1 likely needs the F1 fraction-multiplication or F2 unit-cube foundations.
